concepts.title: Radian Frequency
concepts.one_liner: Radian frequency $w$ is defined as $2 \pi f$, where $f$ is the hertz frequency.
concepts.content: In this book, we use the **radian frequency** for continuous signals, $w = 2 \pi f$, where $f$ is the **hertz frequency**. For a sinusoidal wave of period $T$ seconds, its frequency is $w=2\pi / T$.
concepts.motivation_md: Radian frequency simplifies many mathematical expressions in signal processing, particularly those involving trigonometric functions and Fourier transforms, by incorporating the $2\pi$ factor directly into the frequency term.
concepts.recap_md: - Radian frequency is calculated as $w = 2 \pi f$.

concepts.title: Hertz Frequency
concepts.one_liner: Hertz frequency $f$ represents the number of cycles per second in a signal.
concepts.content: In this book, we use the **radian frequency** for continuous signals, $w = 2 \pi f$, where $f$ is the **hertz frequency**. For a sinusoidal wave of period $T$ seconds, its frequency is $w=2\pi / T$.
concepts.motivation_md: Hertz frequency is the standard unit for measuring cycles per second, providing an intuitive physical measure of how often a periodic event repeats.
concepts.recap_md: - Hertz frequency $f$ is related to radian frequency by $w = 2 \pi f$.

concepts.title: Delta Train (Impulse Train, Dirac Comb)
concepts.one_liner: The delta train is a periodic signal composed of delta impulses centered at regular intervals $nT_s$.
concepts.content:
The **delta train** distribution (also known as the **impulse train** or **Dirac comb**) is a periodic signal, with period $T_s$, composed of delta impulses centered at times $nT_s$. It is defined as:

$$
\delta_{T_s}(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t-n T_s)
$$

When $T_s = 1$, the delta train has the following shape:

(see figure: Delta train with period $T_s=1$. The arrows show when the train's value is infinite. The height of each impulse represents its area.)
concepts.motivation_md: The delta train serves as a mathematical bridge between continuous-time signals and discrete-time samples, allowing the sampling process to be modeled as a multiplication in the time domain.
concepts.recap_md: - The delta train is defined as $\delta_{T_s}(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t-n T_s)$.

concepts.title: Modeling the Sampling Process
concepts.one_liner: The sampling process is modeled by multiplying a continuous function by a delta train to obtain a sampled version.
concepts.content:
The delta train can be used to model the sampling process. Using the sampling property of the delta distribution $\ell (t) \delta (t-a) = \ell(a)$, if we multiply a function, $\ell(t)$, by the delta train, $\delta_{T_s}(t)$, we obtain its sampled version at times $nT_s$, denoted as $\ell_{\delta} (t)$:

$$
\ell_{\delta}  (t) = \ell(t) \delta_{T_s}(t) = \ell(t) \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t-n T_s)  =  \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_s [ n ] \delta(t-n T_s)
$$

The plots in @fig-sampling_signal_using_train show a continuous function and its sampled version using the delta train.

(see figure: Sampling a signal using the delta train.)
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling sampling as multiplication by a delta train allows engineers to use continuous-time Fourier analysis to understand the frequency-domain consequences of discretization.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling is modeled by $\ell_{\delta}(t) = \ell(t) \delta_{T_s}(t)$.

slots.key_passage: - Sampling is modeled by $\ell_{\delta}(t) = \ell(t) \delta_{T_s}(t)$.

concepts.title: Delta-Sampled Function
concepts.one_liner: The delta-sampled function $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ represents discrete signal information over a continuous domain.
concepts.content: The delta-sampled function $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ is a very special function that contains the same amount of information as the discrete signal $\ell_s  [ n ]$ but that is defined over the continuous domain $t$. In fact, the Fourier transform of $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ and $\ell_s  [ n ]$ are closely related.
concepts.motivation_md: This function provides a mathematical representation of samples that exists in continuous time, enabling the use of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform to analyze discrete data.
concepts.recap_md: - $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ contains the same information as the discrete signal $\ell_s [n]$.

slots.motivation: This function provides a mathematical representation of samples that exists in continuous time, enabling the use of the Continuous-Time Fourier Transform to analyze discrete data.
slots.key_passage: - $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ contains the same information as the discrete signal $\ell_s [n]$.

concepts.title: Sampling in the Fourier Domain
concepts.one_liner: Sampling in the time domain results in a periodic summation of the signal's spectrum in the frequency domain.
concepts.content:
The continuous Fourier transform of the delta-sampled function $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ can be computed as the convolution of the Fourier transforms of $\ell(t)$ and the delta train $\delta_{T_s}(t)$. The Fourier transform of a delta comb is also an impulse train, but with frequency spacing that grows as time spacing decreases:

$$
\delta_{T_s}(t) \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \delta_{\frac{2 \pi}{T_s}}(w)
$$

[FIGURE:fe58e7c77a4e1cca | Delta train with period $T_s$.]

[FIGURE:0522d20216d13776 | Fourier transform of delta train.]

Therefore, the continuous Fourier transform of $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ is:

$$
\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w) = \mathscr{L}(w) \circ \frac{2\pi}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta \left(w-k \frac{2 \pi}{T_s} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L} \left(w-k \frac{2 \pi}{T_s} \right)
$$

This shows that $\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w)$ is an infinite sum of translated copies of $\mathscr{L}(w)$. If $T_s$ is small (fast sampling), the copies are far apart; if $T_s$ is large, the copies overlap and mix, producing aliasing.

(see figure: Sketch to illustrate aliasing. Example of a band-limited signal, with frequency content only inside the interval (-w_max, w_max). (a) Sampled with a sampling period such a that T_s <...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the Fourier transform of a sampled signal is critical for identifying aliasing and determining the minimum sampling rate required to preserve signal integrity.
concepts.recap_md: - The Fourier transform of a sampled signal is a sum of shifted copies of the original spectrum.

concepts.title: Nyquist Limit and Spectral Overlap
concepts.one_liner: The Nyquist limit is reached when the spectral copies of a sampled signal begin to overlap, occurring when $T_s > \pi/w_{max}$.
concepts.content: The Nyquist limit is reached when the maximum frequency, $w_{max}$, with spectral content in $\mathscr{L} (w)$ overlaps with its translated copy. This overlap occurs when the sampling period, $T_s$, is $T_s > \pi/w_{max}$. To avoid aliasing, the sampling period has to be shorter than $\pi/w_{max}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept defines the fundamental boundary for perfect signal capture, ensuring that the original information can be recovered without distortion from overlapping frequencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Aliasing is avoided if the sampling period $T_s < \pi/w_{max}$.

slots.motivation: This concept defines the fundamental boundary for perfect signal capture, ensuring that the original information can be recovered without distortion from overlapping frequencies.

concepts.title: Ideal Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Ideal reconstruction recovers a continuous signal from samples using a zero-phase box filter in the frequency domain.
concepts.content:
When the Nyquist condition is satisfied, it is possible to reconstruct the original continuous signal from the samples. This is achieved by applying a box filter that has a constant gain for all frequencies inside $w \in \left[-\pi / T_s, \pi / T_s \right]$, and 0 outside, with a phase of zero:

$$
H(w) = 
 \begin{cases}
    \frac{T_s}{2\pi}       & \quad \text{if } w \in \left[-\pi / T_s, \pi / T_s \right]\\
    0       & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
  \end{cases}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Ideal reconstruction provides the theoretical mechanism for perfectly restoring a continuous signal from its discrete samples by isolating the original spectral copy.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstruction requires a box filter $H(w)$ with gain $T_s/2\pi$ in the range $[-\pi/T_s, \pi/T_s]$.

slots.motivation: Ideal reconstruction provides the theoretical mechanism for perfectly restoring a continuous signal from its discrete samples by isolating the original spectral copy.
slots.key_passage: - Reconstruction requires a box filter $H(w)$ with gain $T_s/2\pi$ in the range $[-\pi/T_s, \pi/T_s]$.

concepts.title: sampling
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one to enable computer processing.
concepts.content: In nature, most of the signals we measure, such as sound and light, are defined over continuous domains like time and space. In order to process these signals with computers, we need to transform the continuous domain into a discrete one. Sampling is the specific process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.
concepts.motivation_md: Computers operate on discrete data, but the physical world is continuous. Sampling provides the bridge necessary to represent real-world phenomena like audio or images in a digital format.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling converts continuous-domain signals into discrete-domain representations.

slots.motivation: Computers operate on discrete data, but the physical world is continuous. Sampling provides the bridge necessary to represent real-world phenomena like audio or images in a digital format.
slots.key_passage: - Sampling converts continuous-domain signals into discrete-domain representations.

concepts.title: sampling period
concepts.one_liner: The sampling period is the fixed time interval between consecutive samples taken from a continuous signal.
concepts.content: Consider a one-dimensional (1D) continuous time signal $\ell (t)$ and its sampled version $\ell [n] = \ell(n T_s)$, where $T_s$ is the sampling period. In this sampling process, some information will naturally get lost. To ensure information is preserved, one can decrease $T_s$, resulting in a more accurate approximation of the continuous signal $\ell (t)$. However, decreasing $T_s$ increases the memory needed to store $\ell [n]$ and the computational cost of processing it. Therefore, choosing the appropriate $T_s$ is essential for finding optimal sampling parameters and allowing for the reconstruction of the original continuous signal.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing the sampling period involves a trade-off: a smaller period captures more detail but requires more storage and processing power. Understanding this parameter is key to efficient digital signal representation.
concepts.recap_md: - The sampling period $T_s$ defines the interval at which a continuous signal is measured.

slots.motivation: Choosing the sampling period involves a trade-off: a smaller period captures more detail but requires more storage and processing power. Understanding this parameter is key to efficient digital signal representation.

concepts.title: aliasing
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing is the confusion of frequencies that occurs when a signal is sampled too sparsely, causing high-frequency components to appear as lower frequencies.
concepts.content:
## Aliasing

Aliasing occurs when a signal is discretized in a way that causes different frequencies to become indistinguishable. For example, consider a continuous signal $\ell (t)=\cos (wt)$ with $w=18\pi$, which has a period of $T=1/9$.

(see figure: Continuous cosine wave, $\ell (t)=\cos (wt)$, with frequency $w=18\pi$.)

If we sample this signal with a period of $T_s=1/11$, we get a discrete signal $\ell [n]$. Although there are more samples than periods in a given interval, the resulting samples do not uniquely constrain the original signal.

(see figure: Sampling the cosine wave with a sampling period of $T_s=1/11$.)

When reconstructing the continuous signal from these samples, infinite possibilities exist. In the absence of prior information, we typically assume the most likely signal is the slowest and smoothest one.

(see figure: There are infinite waves (only two shown) that perfectly pass by all the samples.)

Under this "slow and smooth" prior, the samples of the $T=1/9$ signal may appear to correspond to a cosine function with a lower frequency (e.g., $T=1/2$). This confusion of frequencies is called aliasing.
concepts.motivation_md: Aliasing is a fundamental distortion in digital systems. It explains why wagon wheels might appear to spin backward in movies or why fine patterns on a shirt can create 'moir�' effects on camera.
concepts.recap_md: - Aliasing is the phenomenon where high-frequency signals become indistinguishable from lower-frequency ones after sampling.

concepts.title: slow and smooth prior
concepts.one_liner: The slow and smooth prior is the assumption that, among infinite possible signals passing through a set of samples, the most likely original signal is the one with the lowest frequency and smoothest trajectory.
concepts.content:
When reconstructing an original continuous signal from its discrete samples $\ell [n]$, the samples themselves do not constrain what happens between them, leading to infinite possible reconstructions. In the absence of other information, we assume that the most likely signal is the slowest and smoothest signal.

(see figure: There are infinite waves (only two shown) that perfectly pass by all the samples.)

Under this slow and smooth prior, samples may be interpreted as a lower frequency signal than the actual input. For instance, a signal with period $T=1/9$ might be reconstructed as one with $T=1/2$ if the sampling is insufficient. Human perception also seems to follow this assumption; we have an inherent prior towards smooth and slow trajectories and textures, and our visual system tends to follow this prior when faced with noise or missing information.
concepts.motivation_md: Because discrete samples are ambiguous, we need a mathematical or perceptual 'tie-breaker' to decide what the signal looks like between samples. The slow and smooth prior provides a natural default that aligns with how the physical world usually behaves.
concepts.recap_md: - This prior assumes the original signal is the smoothest and lowest-frequency version that fits the samples.

concepts.title: Band-limited Signal
concepts.one_liner: A band-limited signal is a signal that contains no spectral content above a specific maximum frequency.
concepts.content:
A band-limited signal $\ell (t)$ is defined as a signal that has no spectral content above a certain frequency $w_{max}$. This means its Fourier transform is zero for all frequencies higher than $w_{max}$.

(see figure: A band-limited signal with maximum frequency $w_{max}$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Most real-world signals have a limit to how fast they can fluctuate. Defining a signal as band-limited allows us to apply the Sampling Theorem to determine exactly how many samples are needed to capture it perfectly.
concepts.recap_md: - A signal is band-limited if its Fourier transform is zero for all frequencies $|w| > w_{max}$.

slots.motivation: Most real-world signals have a limit to how fast they can fluctuate. Defining a signal as band-limited allows us to apply the Sampling Theorem to determine exactly how many samples are needed to capture it perfectly.
slots.key_passage: - A signal is band-limited if its Fourier transform is zero for all frequencies $|w| > w_{max}$.

(see figure: A band-limited signal with maximum frequency $w_{max}$.)

concepts.title: Sampling Theorem (Nyquist Theorem)
concepts.one_liner: The Sampling Theorem states that a signal can be perfectly reconstructed if the sampling frequency is more than twice the signal's maximum frequency.
concepts.content:
The sampling theorem, also known as the Nyquist theorem, states that for a signal to be perfectly reconstructed from a set of samples (under the slow and smooth prior), the sampling frequency $w_s = 2 \pi /T_s$ must satisfy $w_s > 2w_{max}$, where $w_{max}$ is the maximum frequency present in the input signal.

The theorem can also be expressed in terms of the sampling period $T_s$. The sampling period must be smaller than half of the period of the highest frequency component: $T_s < T_{min} / 2$, where $T_{min} = 2 \pi /w_{max}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem is the foundation of all digital media. It provides the exact mathematical requirement for digitizing a signal (like audio on a CD) such that it can be converted back to its original continuous form without any loss of information.
concepts.recap_md: - Perfect reconstruction requires a sampling frequency $w_s > 2w_{max}$.

concepts.title: Nyquist Condition
concepts.one_liner: The Nyquist condition is the requirement that the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in a signal to avoid aliasing.
concepts.content:
The Nyquist condition is the requirement established by the sampling theorem for perfect signal reconstruction. It states that the sampling frequency $w_s = 2 \pi /T_s$ must be greater than twice the maximum frequency $w_{max}$ of the input signal ($w_s > 2w_{max}$).

In terms of the sampling period $T_s$, the condition requires that $T_s < T_{min} / 2$, meaning the sampling period must be smaller than half the period of the highest frequency component ($T_{min} = 2 \pi /w_{max}$). If this condition is not met, the signal cannot be perfectly reconstructed and aliasing may occur.
concepts.motivation_md: The Nyquist condition acts as a 'speed limit' for sampling. It tells engineers exactly how fast they need to sample a signal to ensure the digital version remains faithful to the original.
concepts.recap_md: - The condition is satisfied when $w_s > 2w_{max}$ or $T_s < T_{min} / 2$.

concepts.title: Sinc Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Sinc interpolation is the optimal reconstruction of a slow and smooth signal from its samples in terms of the $L^2$ norm.
concepts.content:
When no other prior information is available about the function $\ell(t)$, and under the slow and smooth prior, the optimal reconstruction in terms of the $L^2$ norm is given by the sinc function:

$$
\begin{split}
\text{sinc} (t/T_s) & = \text{argmin}_{h(t)} \int \left( \ell(t) - \ell_{\delta} (t) \circ h(t) \right)^2 dt \\
& = \text{argmin}_{h(t)} \int \left( \mathscr{L}(w) - \mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w) H(w) \right) ^2 dw
\end{split}
$$

Then the function $\widetilde \ell(t)$ that best approximates the input signal from its samples $\ell_s[n]$ is:

$$
\widetilde \ell(t) =  \ell_{\delta} (t) \circ \text{sinc} (t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_s[n] \text{sinc} \left(\frac{t-nT_s}{T_s} \right)
$$

where $\widetilde \ell(t)$ is the reconstructed signal. The linear superposition of all the scaled and shifted sincs produces a smooth interpolation of the sampled function, where the zero crossings of each sinc coincide with the sample locations.

(see figure: Smooth interpolation of the sampled function using sinc functions.)
concepts.motivation_md: Sinc interpolation provides a mathematically optimal way to reconstruct a continuous signal from discrete samples when the signal is band-limited, minimizing the error between the original and reconstructed functions.
concepts.recap_md: - It is the optimal reconstruction method for slow and smooth signals in terms of the $L^2$ norm.

slots.motivation: Sinc interpolation provides a mathematically optimal way to reconstruct a continuous signal from discrete samples when the signal is band-limited, minimizing the error between the original and reconstructed functions.
slots.key_passage: - It is the optimal reconstruction method for slow and smooth signals in terms of the $L^2$ norm.
slots.example:
When no other prior information is available about the function $\ell(t)$, and under the slow and smooth prior, the optimal reconstruction in terms of the $L^2$ norm is given by the sinc function:

$$
\begin{split}
\text{sinc} (t/T_s) & = \text{argmin}_{h(t)} \int \left( \ell(t) - \ell_{\delta} (t) \circ h(t) \right)^2 dt \\
& = \text{argmin}_{h(t)} \int \left( \mathscr{L}(w) - \mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w) H(w) \right) ^2 dw
\end{split}
$$

Then the function $\widetilde \ell(t)$ that best approximates the input signal from its samples $\ell_s[n]$ is:

$$
\widetilde \ell(t) =  \ell_{\delta} (t) \circ \text{sinc} (t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_s[n] \text{sinc} \left(\frac{t-nT_s}{T_s} \right)
$$

where $\widetilde \ell(t)$ is the reconstructed signal. The linear superposition of all the scaled and shifted sincs produces a smooth interpolation of the sampled function, where the zero crossings of each sinc coincide with the sample locations.

(see figure: Smooth interpolation of the sampled function using sinc functions.)

concepts.title: Time-Limited vs. Frequency Band-Limited Tradeoff
concepts.one_liner: A signal cannot be simultaneously time-limited and frequency band-limited.
concepts.content: A signal cannot be simultaneously time-limited and frequency band-limited. For any time-limited signal (i.e., a signal that is defined inside an interval $t \in \left[a,b \right]$ and is zero outside), the Fourier transform is not band-limited.
concepts.motivation_md: This principle establishes a fundamental limit in signal processing, showing that any signal with a finite duration must have an infinite frequency spectrum, and vice versa.
concepts.recap_md: - Signals cannot be bounded in both the time and frequency domains at once.

concepts.title: 2D Ideal Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: The 2D ideal interpolation function is a separable product of sinc functions along two spatial dimensions.
concepts.content:
All the derivations for ideal reconstruction extend naturally to 2D because all the functions are separable along the two spatial dimensions. In two dimensions, the ideal interpolation function is:

$$
\text{sinc} (x,y)  = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x} \frac{\sin (\pi y)}{\pi y}
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Extending 1D sampling theory to 2D allows for the perfect reconstruction of images and other spatial data from discrete grids.
concepts.recap_md: - 2D ideal reconstruction relies on the separability of the interpolation functions.

concepts.title: Nearest Neighbor Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Nearest neighbor interpolation assigns each time instant the value of the closest sample in time.
concepts.content:
Nearest interpolation consists of assigning to each time instant the value of the nearest sample in time. This can be written as a linear convolution of the sampled signal $\ell_\delta (t)$ with a box kernel of width $T_s$.

(see figure: (top) Nearest interpolation. (bottom) Linear interpolation. Both interpolation methods can be modeled by a convolution with the kernel shown in the middle (a box and a triangle).)
concepts.motivation_md: It is the simplest and fastest interpolation method, used when computational efficiency is prioritized over reconstruction smoothness.
concepts.recap_md: - Assigns values based on the closest temporal sample.

concepts.title: Linear Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Linear interpolation estimates values by interpolating linearly between two consecutive samples.
concepts.content:
Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values. This can be written as a linear convolution with a triangle kernel $h(t)$ of width $2T_s$.

(see figure: (top) Nearest interpolation. (bottom) Linear interpolation. Both interpolation methods can be modeled by a convolution with the kernel shown in the middle (a box and a triangle).)
concepts.motivation_md: Linear interpolation provides a smoother result than nearest neighbor interpolation by assuming a constant rate of change between samples.

concepts.title: Lanczos-1 Interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Lanczos-1 interpolation uses only the central lobe of the sinc function as its kernel.
concepts.content: Lanczos-1 interpolation consists of using as kernel only the central lobe of the sinc function. This provides an interpolation that is smooth using only a local neighborhood. Other interpolation methods such as cubic interpolation can also be written as convolutions.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a smooth, local approximation of the ideal sinc interpolation, avoiding the infinite computation required by the full sinc function.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the central lobe of the sinc function as a local kernel.

concepts.title: 2D Rectangular Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Rectangular sampling is a 2D sampling pattern where a continuous image is sampled on a regular grid.
concepts.content:
If we have a continuous image $\ell (x,y)$ we can sample it using a rectangular grid as $\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (nT_x, mT_y)$. This is a specific case of the general 2D sampling pattern $\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$ where the constants are set to $a=T, b=0, c=0, d=T$.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Rectangular sampling is the standard method for digitizing images, as it directly maps to the grid-like structure of most digital sensors and displays.
concepts.recap_md: - Samples a 2D signal at regular intervals on a grid.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)

concepts.title: 2D Hexagonal Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Hexagonal sampling is a 2D sampling pattern defined by a specific non-rectangular coordinate transformation.
concepts.content:
In 2D sampling, we can define a discrete image as $\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$ where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. If we set $a=T_1, b=-T_2 / 2, c=0, d=T_2$, we obtain a hexagonal sampling pattern.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Hexagonal sampling can be more efficient than rectangular sampling for certain band-limited signals and is used in specific sensor geometries.
concepts.recap_md: - A non-rectangular sampling pattern defined by specific linear combinations of indices.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)

concepts.title: 2D Irregular Sampling
concepts.one_liner: 2D sampling can follow regular rectangular or hexagonal patterns, or occur at random locations known as irregular sampling.
concepts.content: 2D sampling patterns are defined by constants $a,b,c,d$. For instance, if $a=T,b=0,c=0,d=T$, the result is a regular rectangular sampling. Other patterns are possible, such as hexagonal sampling where $a=T_1,b=-T_2 / 2,c=0,d=T_2$. Samples can also be placed at random locations, which is known as irregular sampling. (see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: While rectangular grids are standard for digital displays, different geometric arrangements or random placements can better suit specific sensor designs or reduce certain types of aliasing artifacts.
concepts.recap_md: - Rectangular sampling uses a standard orthogonal grid defined by fixed constants.

concepts.title: Fourier Transform of a 2D Sampled Signal
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a 2D sampled signal is a sum of shifted versions of the continuous signal's transform.
concepts.content: The continuous Fourier transform of a 2D delta train can be calculated by applying a change in variables and using a procedure similar to the 1D case. The result is: $$\Delta_{A} (\mathbf{w}) = \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \delta \left( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} \right)$$ Therefore, the Fourier transform of the sampled signal $\ell_{\delta} (x,y)$ is: $$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (\mathbf{w}) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \mathscr{L} \left( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} \right)$$ {#eq-genericsampling}
concepts.motivation_md: To understand how sampling affects the frequency content of an image, we need a mathematical expression for the Fourier transform of the sampled signal in terms of the original signal's spectrum.
concepts.recap_md: - The transform consists of periodic replications of the original signal's spectrum.

slots.example: The continuous Fourier transform of a 2D delta train can be calculated by applying a change in variables and using a procedure similar to the 1D case. The result is: $$\Delta_{A} (\mathbf{w}) = \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \delta \left( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} \right)$$ Therefore, the Fourier transform of the sampled signal $\ell_{\delta} (x,y)$ is: $$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (\mathbf{w}) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \mathscr{L} \left( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} \right)$$ {#eq-genericsampling}

concepts.title: Aliasing in 2D Images
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing in 2D images occurs when sampling at insufficient frequencies, causing visual artifacts like changing stripe orientations.
concepts.content: Sampling with the wrong frequency has interesting effects in 2D. For example, a picture downsampled at different resolutions (such as 103×128 or 26×32) and then reconstructed to the original resolution shows the effects of aliasing. The stripes on a zebra's body may change orientation as they are downsampled, and at very low resolutions, the subject may become unrecognizable. These effects occur because the Fourier transform of the sampled signal changes substantially from one resolution to the next due to overlapping spectral replications. ![Subsampling with aliasing. (a) The zebra sampled with aliasing starts looking like a cow. (b) Fourier transform of the continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$ multiplied by delta trains: $\ell_{\delta}(x,y)$. (c) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding sampled signals, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. (d) Fourier transform of the reconstructed signal with aliasing. (e) Sampled image after processing it with an anti-aliasing filter. (f) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding anti-aliased sampled images, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. Note that now the central part of the Fourier transform is not changing.](figures/Image_processing_sampling/aliasing_ft_abc1.png){width=100% #fig-aliasingFTzebra}
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding aliasing is crucial for digital imaging to prevent distortions and artifacts that occur when a signal is sampled below the Nyquist rate.
concepts.recap_md: - Aliasing occurs when high-frequency components are incorrectly mapped to lower frequencies during sampling.

concepts.title: Anti-Aliasing Filter
concepts.one_liner: An anti-aliasing filter is a low-pass filter applied before sampling to make a signal band-limited and prevent high-frequency interference.
concepts.content: In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. This allows us to sample the signal while avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image. While the anti-aliasing filter prevents artifacts, it does not prevent the loss of information contained in the high spatial frequencies. The anti-aliasing filter can be a box filter with support equal to the desired sampling region in the frequency domain.
concepts.motivation_md: Without pre-filtering, high-frequency noise and details "fold back" into the visible spectrum as artifacts; filtering ensures the sampled signal is a clean representation of the base frequencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Low-pass filtering before sampling ensures the signal obeys the Nyquist criterion.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal sampling extends sampling theory to include the time dimension, explaining effects like the perceived reversal of rotating objects in video.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal sampling can be studied using generic sampling equations applied to the $N$-dimensional case. Temporal aliasing is responsible for typical illusions, such as seeing wheels or fans change their sense of rotation in movies. To avoid these artifacts, it is important to apply an anti-aliasing filter before sampling in the temporal domain.
concepts.motivation_md: Video is a 3D signal consisting of spatial dimensions and time; understanding its sampling is necessary to prevent motion artifacts and ensure smooth playback.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling occurs across both spatial coordinates and the time axis.

concepts.title: Global Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Global shutter mode is a regular sampling method where all pixels in a 2D grid are exposed simultaneously at regular time intervals.
concepts.content: The most common type of spatiotemporal sampling is regular sampling, also called global shutter mode. In this mode, all pixels are sampled in a regular spatial 2D grid and at regular time instants in which all the pixels are exposed simultaneously.
concepts.motivation_md: Global shutters are ideal for capturing fast-moving objects without geometric distortion, as every part of the image represents the exact same moment in time.
concepts.recap_md: - All pixels are captured at the exact same instant in time.

concepts.title: Rolling Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Rolling shutter mode samples image rows sequentially at different times, which can cause spatial distortions when capturing moving objects.
concepts.content: Rolling shutter mode is a commonly used sampling method in many cameras, such as DSLRs and mobile phones. In this mode, every row in the image is sampled simultaneously, but different rows are sampled at different instants. This mode allows for faster sampling rates with current hardware implementations, but it can create spatial distortions in the image if the camera moves or when taking pictures of moving objects.
concepts.motivation_md: Rolling shutters are efficient to implement in CMOS sensors, allowing for high-resolution capture, though they introduce artifacts like "jello" effects during motion.
concepts.recap_md: - Rows are sampled sequentially rather than all at once.

concepts.title: Moire Patterns
concepts.one_liner: Moire patterns are interference patterns that occur when overlapping semitransparent patterns create new, unintended visual structures.
concepts.content: Moire patterns, also related to aliasing, are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other. [FIGURE:c1949ca908869fea | A moiré pattern created by two overlapping sets of parallel black lines. One set of lines is perfectly vertical, while the second set is rotated at a slight angle, creating a visual interference...]
concepts.motivation_md: Moire patterns illustrate the visual consequences of frequency interference, often occurring in digital photography when a fine pattern in a scene interacts with the camera's pixel grid.
concepts.recap_md: - These patterns result from the superposition of two or more periodic structures.

prereq.rationale: The sampling period is the primary parameter that defines the temporal resolution of the sampling process.

The occurrence of aliasing depends on the relationship between the signal frequency and the sampling period.
The slow and smooth prior is introduced as a necessary assumption to resolve the ambiguity (infinite possibilities) created by aliasing.
The Sampling Theorem specifically applies to band-limited signals.
The Nyquist condition is the core mathematical requirement stated by the Sampling Theorem.
The condition is often expressed in terms of the sampling period Ts.

This technique analyzes the Fourier transform of the delta-sampled function.
